newsitem.title: KENYA: East African flower exports seen on rapid increase.
newsitem.headline: East African flower exports seen on rapid increase.

text.p: Dutch's biggest flower auctions are expecting flower imports from Eastern and Southern African countries to continue to rapidly increase as seen in the last few years, auction officials said.

"Our imports from Africa have increased by more than 10 percent a year in the last few seasons, especially from Kenya." said Albert Haasnoot, direct sales account manager for the BloemenVeiling Flora Rijnsburg-based auction.

"While Tanzania, Uganda and Zambia are still small, they have good potential with a little more work done in infrastructure," Haasnoot told Reuters at the end this weekend of Kenya's three-day horticultural trade exhibition, Hortec '97.
He said that of Flora's auction's total annual turnover of $390 million some 20 percent of the flowers traded were imported, out of which 27 percent came from Kenya.

"Imports are growing fast and within the next five years 30 percent of our flowers will be imports. We are focusing mainly on Africa with Kenya being our overall second biggest import source after Israel.
"But from next season we are going to focus on the markets in Tanzania and Zambia which we will provide advice and support for," Haasnoot said.
He said Flora regards the East African market of such importance, that the auction recently opened a local representative office in Nairobi.
About 90 percent of Kenya's horticultural production is shipped out of Nairobi by air, with cut flowers accounting up 45 percent of the total output.
The industry has seen a rapid growth in recent years and total production of flowers, fruits and vegetables saw a jump to over 84,000 tonnes in 1996, up from some 75,000 tonnes in 1995.

BloemenVeiling Aalsmeer, the largest of the Netherland's seven flower auctions with an annual turnover of $1.3 billion, agreed the trend in Holland was in favour of increased imports from East Africa.
About 19 percent of Aalsmeer's flowers are imported, of which some 40 percent are from Africa, mostly Kenya and Zimbabwe, but with increasing volumes coming from Zambia, Tanzania and Uganda.

"We are watching the development with interest. Up to now imports have been growing quite fast, with about one percent a year in the last few years, and while it doesn't sound of much, it's a lot in terms of quantity," said Dich van Dam of Aalsmeer's import department.

Van Dam said that Aalsmeer expects the general consumption of cut flowers in the European markets to increase by up to five percent within the next few years, mostly due to the increasing sales of flowers in super market chains.

Feico Smit, Africa area manager for BloemenVeiling Holland, said that with the competitive low costs of producing flowers in Africa, compared to in Europe and Israel, the potential for East African countries to further expand was enormous.

"If they can produce something at lower costs here in Africa then you will see some of the Dutch growers disappear from the market, with the exemption of specialised varieties, and you will see a shift towards the countries here," said Smit.
But he noted that any big-scale increase would be strongly dependent on the development of a reliable air freight market with direct transport links to Europe.
The Holland auction is the second biggest of the country's seven flower auctions with an annual turnover of some $1.1 billion in 1996. --Reuters Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44-171-542-7706 Fax+5017
